newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels want talks moved from Chiapas state.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels want talks moved from Chiapas state.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-11-12

text.p: Mexico's Zapatista rebels on Tuesday demanded that peace talks with the federal government be moved to outside the southern state of Chiapas, where it said the state government was waging a campaign of repression.

Rebel leaders said the state government was "sabotaging" the peace process by cracking down on peasants supporting the Zapatistas, who first took up in arms in 1994 in search of Indian rights and democracy in this impoverished state.
Peace talks between the federal government and rebels have been on hold since September, when the rebels pulled out after accusing negotiators of being racists.
"The Chiapas government does not want peace," Commander Tacho, a military leader of the mostly Indian rebel movement, told a news conference.

"By murder, kicking peasants off their lands, torture and disappearances the government of Chiapas ... wants to make this peace process fail," said the leader, who wore one of the rebels' trademark ski-masks to hide his identity.
Rebels blamed the state government for the deaths of three peasants last weekend during a clash between farmers and state police.

The rebels met on Tuesday with delegates from a legislative commission known as Cocopa that is acting as a go-between between the government and rebels in order to get the 19-month-long peace process restarted. Both sides discussed installing a special commission to oversee peace accords once they are signed.
Another rebel leader, Commander David, suggested the peace process be moved to Mexico City, Washington D.C., or Europe.
Government negotiators have to date refused to allow peace talks to be moved anywhere outside of Chiapas. Mexico's government has said the conflict is a local, not national, issue.
